title: The chunking trade-off: Context vs. precision
text: Jambo, I'm Vedanshi Dakshash Patel. Chapter 3 gave us embeddings, text compared by meaning instead of by wording, but it left one question wide open. A piece of text of what size? A sentence, a page, the whole document? The model doesn't care. Retrieval cares enormously. Here is the whole idea in one breath. Chunking is a design decision where you cut a document decides what retrieval

title: Fixed character counts vs. structure-aware splitting
text: Averaging them. So, cut it smaller, but this trade-off runs in both directions. Too small and a chunk loses the context that gave it meaning. Five days per year is useless if you cannot tell five days of what. Too large and you have rebuilt the whole document problem in miniature. There is no correct number to look up. title: Prompting Claude to evaluate your document chunking strategy
text: Page, three cuts, only two of them respect what is written. How the tooling actually does it? Try a prioritized list of separators. Paragraph breaks first, then line breaks, then individual spaces. Drop to a smaller unit only when the larger one would produce an oversized chunk, so paragraphs stay whole whenever they possibly can. LangChain's recursive splitter is one example of the pattern. The pattern is the point, not the library. Predict before I show you 140-page benefits manual. One question, how many vacation days do I get in my second year? Now, chunk that manual three ways as one whole document by fixed character count or a paragraph and heading boundaries. Which one puts the complete answer inside a single chunk? Whole document, the question matches one

Vector carrying the entire manual. You retrieve everything or you cannot tell this manual from the next one. Fixed count, the vacation table splits mid-row and the sentence naming the policy lands in a different chunk from the number it refers to. Structure aware, the vacation section stays whole, second year increase included. Let's recap. A whole document embedded as one vector averages every topic it contains, so no single question matches it sharply. Chunk size fails in both directions. Too small loses context, too large loses precision. Overlap is a guard with a clear rationale and an unsettled payoff. And splitting at the document's own boundaries beats splitting at arbitrary counts. Chunking is a design decision. And chapter five asks the next one, how do you search thousands

Of these chunks fast? Your turn, paste this. Here's a document I actually work with. I'll describe its structure. Propose a chunking strategy, approximate size, whether to use overlap, and where the boundaries should fall. Then argue the opposite case as strongly as you can and tell me which failure would cost me more, a chunk too small to carry its context or one too large to match precisely. That second half is the part that matters. Anything will hand you a confident first answer. Making it argue against itself is how you find out whether the recommendation was reasoned or reflexive. Bring a document whose structure you already know and see whether its boundaries match the ones you would have drawn. Where you cut the page, Vedant Sudhaksh Patel.
